Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00141

This completion does not take place in the outside world, since the two are one in existence there. Things that are one in existence cannot bring each other into existence. Rather, the mind divides a specific kind into two parts in thought and judges one to be the cause of the other. This is because the parts of one essence depend on each other. The part that is needed, and so serves as cause, can only be the distinguishing feature. The general kind cannot cause the distinguishing feature to exist. If it did, it would have to bring about every opposing distinguishing feature, so one thing would contain opposites that cannot coexist. That is impossible. So the distinguishing feature must cause the general kind to exist as a specific kind. It divides the general nature taken without restriction, brings about the particular share of that nature found in the specific kind, and forms one part of the whole along with what distinguishes that kind from others.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00142

A possible objection is this: if rationality causes animal nature in general, it cannot divide that nature into kinds. But if it causes a particular kind of animal, such as a human being, that kind must already be specific before rationality can cause it. Once it is specific, however, it already exists and no longer needs a cause. The answer is that the distinguishing feature comes before the general kind because it causes the kind’s nature. The effect cannot first demand its cause, because it has not yet come into existence at the level of the cause. It is the cause that brings the effect into existence. In the same way, animal nature does not call for one particular feature. It needs some feature, but does not choose which one. Rationality, by its own nature, brings about this particular kind of animal. The general need comes from animal nature; the precise feature that meets that need comes from the distinguishing feature. Nor is it strange for one general kind to have several causes, since its unity is weak.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00143

It is strange that the author of The Eastern Discussions, though he understood this point, failed to use it in his argument for matter. After giving his proof, he says he presented it to many sharp thinkers, and none found fault with its steps. His argument for matter in the celestial sphere goes like this: the sphere has a fixed size and shape because it cannot come to be or pass away. What makes this necessary? It must be the sphere’s bodily nature, a feature within it, or something separate from it. It cannot be its bodily nature: then all bodies would have the same size and shape. It cannot be a feature within it either, since we would then have to ask the same question about that feature. And it cannot be something separate, because that would relate equally to all bodies. So the sphere’s fixed size and shape must come from the underlying matter that receives its bodily form. That was meant to establish matter. But the sphere’s specific form comes before bodily nature in the order of existence. It gives the sphere its distinguishing feature and makes the general kind, body, specific. So it can cause the sphere’s particular size and shape. None of the problems he named follows. Keep this point in mind.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00144
Chapter 7 — How form joins with matter
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00145

The word “form” can refer to a specific kind of thing, or to the nature of any thing. It can also mean what gives a thing its underlying reality, what makes matter into a natural kind, or a perfection that can exist apart from a thing. If we look closely at all these uses, we find that they share one basic meaning: what makes a thing actually be what it is. That is why there is no contradiction in saying both that a thing’s form is its essence—what makes it what it is—and that its matter is what bears its form.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00146

To see why, start with this: matter in any thing is indeterminate. It has no definite nature in itself; it is only the possibility of becoming something. Form, by contrast, makes a thing actual. It is what makes the thing be something. For example, the matter of a bed is wood, but not wood considered simply as wood. Insofar as it has the nature and definite form of wood, it is already something in its own right, not matter for a bed. It is matter for a bed because it can become a bed, a door, a chair, or something else. Its refusal to take certain other forms comes not from its potential, but from its present actuality: it already has a specific form that prevents it from becoming something whose nature conflicts with its own. So the nature of wood has both an incomplete side and a complete side. Because it is incomplete, it can take on another completion; because it is already complete in one way, it cannot take on a conflicting completion. Together, these two sides explain why a bed has both matter and form.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00147

Likewise, wood has its own form, while its matter is the elements—not considered as earth, water, or something else, but as elements mixed in a way that makes them ready to become a mineral, a plant, an animal, or another particular kind, but not just anything. This continues until we reach matter that has no matter beneath it: first matter, the basic underlying matter of all things. It has no definite nature or actuality apart from being a substance with the potential to become anything, with nothing in itself to make it one thing rather than another. It is only a receiver, with nothing but the capacity to become something; otherwise, the account would lead to a circle or an endless chain. Calling it a substance does not make it definite; it is real only as an open possibility. Its readiness to change is not a completed form, but only the capacity to become one. Nonexistence is different: taken as nonexistence, it has no reality at all—not even an indeterminate reality or the potential to become something. First matter has this one weak kind of reality, and no other on its own. It is the lowest and weakest kind of being, almost at the edge of existence.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00148

From this, a thoughtful reader can see that every composite thing is what it is through what serves as its form, not through what serves as its matter. Matter, as matter, is absorbed into form just as a general kind is absorbed into its distinguishing feature. Matter stands to form as incompleteness to completeness and weakness to strength. A thing’s reality is established by its form. It needs matter so that form can produce its effects and the features that come with them and cannot be separated from them, such as quantity, quality, and place. If form could exist apart from matter, it would still be the same thing, because matter has no independent reality; it is only the potential for reality.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00149

The world is a world through its form, not its matter; a bed is a bed through its shape, not its wood; a human being is human through the soul that guides the body, not through the body alone; and what exists is made real by existence, not by its essence. If the form of the world existed on its own, it would still be a world. If a bed’s shape existed without wood, it would still be a bed. Likewise, the human soul remains human when separated from the body, and existence apart from essence is still existence, as with God, the Necessary Being. The point is captured in the saying that when a person understands how things exist as they truly are, that person becomes an intelligible world, like the world that exists outside the mind. A wisdom poem puts it this way: “A heart full of cattle, donkeys, fields, and estates is just a village, not a heart.” This also helps explain why early logicians allowed a thing to be defined by its ultimate distinguishing feature alone, even though they held that a definition should reveal the thing’s full nature.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00150

An exalted principle is clear from what we have said in this chapter and from hints given earlier. What makes any essence—simple or composite—be what it is and exist is only its ultimate distinguishing feature. The other distinguishing features and forms that go with it are like powers, conditions, tools, and preparatory causes. They ready the essence for the existence it has through that ultimate feature. They do not belong to its final, settled nature or make up the core of its reality, although each may make up a different nature.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00151

For example, some of the powers and forms in the human body prepare first matter simply to be a body, such as the form that gives it extension. Others give it plant life through the powers of nourishment, growth, and reproduction. Others give it animal life through sensation and voluntary movement. Still others make it human through the power of reason. Each earlier form prepares the way for the next. The later form arises from the earlier forms, and they receive their place in the whole through it. What had first been causes, conditions, and preparations later become powers, dependent features, and branches. The final form becomes the source and leading form for all the rest; the others serve it as helpers and offshoots.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00152

From these principles and what follows, it will become clear that a kind’s distinguishing features are not things apart from it. They are the particular ways its true nature exists as real individuals. What exists outside the mind is existence itself. Through sensation or direct awareness, the mind draws broad or narrow concepts from a thing’s own nature, and concepts of its incidental features from other aspects of it. The mind then applies to these concepts what belongs to them in the outside world. A concept drawn from the thing itself is called essential; one drawn from another aspect of it is called incidental. An essential concept belongs directly to what exists, because it is one with that thing in reality. An incidental concept belongs to it only indirectly, as something added. This does not mean that a shared nature exists only in the mind, as one might think. Existence belongs directly to it when the concept is essential: what truly exists is one with that nature in the outside world; the two are not separate realities.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00153
Chapter 8 — How the general kind is taken from matter and the distinguishing feature from form
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00154

In things made of matter and form, the general kind is taken from the matter, and the distinguishing feature from the form. Someone might object: A body, as we shall explain, is made up of matter and form, and both are substances, according to Aristotle and his followers. Yet the nature of a body is an extended substance. Why, then, should we take the concept of “substance” from matter rather than from form? It seems to apply to both equally, since both are kinds of substance.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00155

Here is the answer. Matter and form each have a simple specific nature. In the mind, each can be analyzed into a shared general kind and a distinguishing feature that makes it a specific kind and gives it its existence. This is the concept of substance. The distinguishing feature of matter is its capacity to receive forms; the distinguishing feature of form is extension. Matter is matter because it has the capacity to receive forms, and form is that form because it is extended. But matter’s capacity does not make it an actual, definite thing. It gives matter only the potential to become actual things.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00156

When we consider matter itself, all that makes it definite is that it is a substance. This gives it only the weakest kind of definition. Form is different: the idea of substance is contained within the idea of “extended,” just as a general kind is absorbed into its distinguishing feature. Matter in a body is nothing but substance with the capacity to take on any form or quality. Likewise, a general kind has only the idea of substance, which can in itself be joined with the conditions that make a thing a particular kind or individual. The potentiality in matter corresponds to the possibility found in a general kind. And the form of a body is its extension and continuity, just as its distinguishing feature is the simple concept “extended.” Nothing general or particular is included in that concept, as careful thinkers have explained. When grammarians explain a word formed from a verb, the word “thing” only refers back to the pronoun contained in it; it adds nothing else. Avicenna confirms this in The Healing: when “rational” is used in the broad sense of a distinguishing feature, it means “a thing that has reason.” Calling something “a thing that has reason” does not by itself tell us whether it is a substance or a quality. We know from other considerations that it must be a substance, or a body.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00157

This shows why, in the nature of a body, the concept of “substance” is taken from matter and the distinguishing feature from form. The same applies to other composite things like it. I can make this clearer, so listen closely to what I am about to explain, and keep these secrets from those who would misuse them.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00158

Philosophers agree that a general kind, in relation to its distinguishing feature, is a necessary feature of it, while the distinguishing feature, in relation to the general kind, is a property. They also say that in things made of matter and form, the general kind corresponds to the matter and the distinguishing feature to the form. These claims together imply that the distinguishing features of substances are not themselves substances in the sense of falling under the general kind “substance.” They relate to that general kind as something necessarily accompanying it, not as a kind falling under it. In the same sense, bodily forms and other forms are not substances, even though “substance” can be applied to them in a secondary way. Their not belonging by their own nature to the category of substance does not mean that they must belong to one of the nine categories of qualities. Simple natures, whether outside the mind or in it, do not in themselves fall under any general kind.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00159

This does not challenge the claim that there are ten categories, as Avicenna explains in the Categories section of The Healing. The point is that anything with a specific definition belongs by its own nature to one of these categories. It does not follow that everything must have a definition; that would lead to circular reasoning or an endless chain. Some things are understood directly, not through a definition, such as existence and many things we know through immediate awareness. Someone might object: A human being is made up of a body, which is its matter, and a soul, which is its form. The soul has been proved to be a substance, immaterial and able to survive the body’s destruction, as we shall show. But what you have said about forms applies just as well to the rational soul, since it too is a form and the source of the distinguishing feature in the definition of a human being.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00160

I would answer that the human soul can be considered in two ways: as the body’s form and soul, and as a thing in itself. In the first sense, it exists for something else—the body. In the second, it exists in itself, whether for itself or for something else. For a form that exists in matter, its existence in itself is the same as its existence in the matter. The two ways of considering it therefore coincide. But a form that can exist apart from matter has its own existence in itself. The two ways of considering it, and the two kinds of existence, are then distinct. When a form that exists in matter leaves its matter, it is destroyed. A form that can exist apart from matter may leave it and still continue to exist. Its existence for the matter and its existence in itself are not the same.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00161

Once this is clear, we can say that a thing’s belonging to a category in one respect does not mean it belongs to that category—or to any category—in another respect. The human soul is a substance when considered in itself, but as a soul it is understood through its relation to the body. Considered as part of the body, or as the form that completes it, it need not be a substance in that same sense. The same applies to other forms that exist in matter. It is true that the soul is an immaterial substance. But its role in making up the body does not have to fall under the general kind “substance.” The soul as a self-standing reality is one thing; as a state or form of the body, it is another.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00162

The same answer addresses an objection to the philosophers’ rule that every new thing must be preceded by matter’s readiness to receive it. The rule may seem to conflict with the view that newly created souls are immaterial, a view held by Aristotle, the First Teacher. The human body, through its particular condition, calls for a governing soul to direct it—that is, for something able to perform these tasks. The Generous Giver must therefore bring into existence a source of human guidance and action. Such a source can only be a reality that is immaterial in itself. So the soul does not come into being because the body calls for its essence, but because its essence cannot be separated from the role the body calls for. Through its particular mixture, the body calls for something material; the generosity of the Giver brings about a sacred reality.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00163

Just as one thing can be a substance in one respect and a quality in another, so one thing can be immaterial in its essence and material in its activity. The human soul is immaterial in its essence, but in its activity—guiding and moving the body—it depends on the body and is joined to it. As to its essence, it comes only from the generosity of the Giver. In that respect, it is not preceded by the body’s readiness and does not have to exist together with the body. It is affected by the shortcomings of matter only indirectly. This is my answer to the objection against the rule. Consider it carefully: it may seem clear, yet it has a subtle point. Plato’s claim that the soul is eternal may also be understood in this light.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00164

There is another way to answer. If you reflect on the principles we have already discussed, and remember what the Illuminationist master, Suhrawardi, explains in his two books—that the soul has a simple, luminous reality in The Philosophy of Illumination and is pure existence in The Book of Elucidations—you will see that these mean the same thing. To appear is to be actual, and to be actual is to exist. Illuminationist principles show that light is simple and has no general kind or distinguishing feature. Individual lights differ only in how complete or deficient they are in their luminous existence. You will then understand that separate luminous realities do not fall under the category of substance, even though they exist without being in a subject. My dear reader, hold firmly to this principle: it has a depth that most thinkers have missed. If you study Suhrawardi’s books and the principles he uses to answer objections, an illuminating insight may open to you. From what I have explained, you may already have begun to see that the whole world is existence, all existence is light, and “incidental light is light upon light.”
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00165

Consider the human body, with its forms and powers—the sources of its actions. It is like an army of the luminous governing soul in the world of opposites, and a place where the soul’s lights and effects appear. Those powers and tools, together with their commander, are all pure existence and light: like lamps of different brightness, arranged in order, one above another, all lit by a single light and under its independent command. A weak light cannot shine independently in the presence of a stronger one. The whole world of existence is like this: rays of light from the one Necessary Being, who exists through Himself. All existence comes from the rising of His light and the shining of His presence, as we see in the sun, whose earthly and heavenly image points to Him. But there is a difference between these two kinds of rays. The rays of the sun of intellect are living, aware, speaking, and active. The rays of the sun we see are qualities and lights that belong to something else; they are not alive, aware, or acting in themselves. The details of these ideas will come later, God willing.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00166
In brief: The more actual, noble, and luminous a form is, the more receptive, lowly, and dark the matter that receives it is.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00167

In detail: First matter is the source of lowliness and the center of evil and estrangement. It is an ugly old woman whom a luminous soul encounters only after clothing her in bodily and specific forms, and lighting her with powers and qualities. In this way, she leaves behind her bare potentiality, ugliness, and darkness. Once the soul is joined to matter, it brings about these forms, powers, and qualities. But if the soul departs and the flow of those powers and qualities stops, matter seems to return to its bare state, stripped of every feature and quality. It becomes exposed to fading away and decay, and naturally repulsive and frightening. We see this in the unease people feel when they look at the bodies of the dead, especially when left alone with one in the dark.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00168
Chapter 9 — Platonic Forms and Ideas
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00169

Plato is said to have taught, in many statements that agree with his teacher Socrates, that things have forms in the divine realm. These are sometimes called divine Ideas. They do not perish or decay; they last forever. Only the things that come into being here perish.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00170

In the Metaphysics of The Healing, Avicenna says that some people thought this division meant there were two beings for every kind—two human beings, for example, in the meaning of “human”: one a perishable, visible human, the other an eternal, separate human known by the intellect. They said that each had its own existence. They called the separate existence an “Idea.” They also believed that every natural thing had a separate form, which the intellect receives when it understands it, because what the intellect understands does not perish, while everything we see does. They thought that knowledge and proofs aim at these Forms and reach them. Plato and his teacher Socrates are known for strongly defending this view. They said that “humanity” has one meaning shared by all people, and that it remains even when they perish. This shared meaning cannot be the many changing human beings we see. It must therefore be an intelligible reality that exists apart from them. That is Avicenna’s account.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00171

With God’s help, I will first set out the different ways people have explained Plato’s words, and the objections raised against each explanation. Then I will explain what I take to be the truth about separate Forms and Ideas.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00172

Avicenna explained Plato’s words as meaning that each thing has an essence stripped of its added features, an essence that can take on opposite states. But Plato, whose student was Aristotle, the First Teacher, was far too great a thinker to confuse thinking of an essence apart from its features with an essence existing apart from them. Nor would he confuse considering an essence without deciding whether something is joined to it with requiring that nothing be joined to it. He would not confuse being one in meaning with being one individual in the world. If he had, he would have thought that because all people are “human” in the same sense, there is one human being that exists as one individual in many people.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00173

He would also have missed this: if “human” is considered only as what it is, without any added features such as being one or many, then saying that a human, simply as human, is one, eternal, or anything else that goes beyond the meaning of “human” is a contradiction. And he would have thought that saying “humanity always exists” means that one and the same humanity remains forever. How could that be? These distinctions are clear even to students with some training in philosophy, let alone to thinkers of such stature.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00174

Al-Farabi, the Second Teacher, says in The Reconciliation of the Views of Plato and Aristotle that Plato meant that things have Forms in God’s knowledge, where they remain unchanged. A later thinker developed this explanation. He said that in the world we sense there are individual people, each with a body and particular features. This is the natural human being. But there is also “the human” considered simply in itself, without adding oneness, plurality, or any other feature beyond humanity. This is the meaning that can be said of many people, such as Zayd and Amr. When the mind says “human” of both Zayd and Amr, it turns to a meaning set apart from their particular features. It even sets aside the fact that this meaning is abstract or unrestricted. That meaning must exist somewhere: either outside the mind or in it. If it existed outside the mind, the features that make each person an individual would be added to the essence only afterward. So it must exist in the mind, where it is made into a distinct object of thought by the mind’s own way of considering it. The mind can focus on it without attending to that mental distinction. Since the concept “human” can be said of real substances in a way that identifies them, this thinker concluded that there are intellectual substances in the Intellect that are the essences of things in the world. This, he said, is Plato’s very view.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00175

One might object that Plato is generally said to have taught that intellectual substances exist in reality and are universal essences of the individuals we see. The answer is that by “reality” he may have meant the Intellects, which are the true realities of the sensory world. In Plato’s view, the sensory world is only their shadow. That is the end of this thinker’s account.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00176

This explanation is very unlikely. The reports about Plato and the early philosophers, and the ridicule their Aristotelian followers directed at them, show that they meant the Forms to exist outside the mind and stand on their own, not as features lodged in something else. Plato is even reported to have said that, when free of the body, he saw spheres of light. Hermes is said to have described a spiritual being that taught him, and when he asked who it was, the being replied, “I am your complete nature.” If their words did not clearly point to a separate, individual reality for each kind in the creative world, why would the followers of Aristotle have mocked them with the claim—reported by Al-Farabi—that their view must put lines, surfaces, and spheres inside the Intellects?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00177

Their view would also require movements and orbits of those spheres, knowledge of the stars and of music, harmonious sounds, medicine, geometry, straight and curved measurements, hot and cold things, active and passive qualities, universals and particulars, matter and form, and many other things they found absurd.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00178

Our teacher and master, to whom we owe our learning—may God raise his honor—says in one of his philosophical books that divine decree has two distinct senses: a knowing sense and a real, existing sense. It can mean that something appears in knowledge or takes shape in the intellectual world. It can also mean that it exists outside the mind. We have explained that an actual infinite is impossible in the realm of divine measure: divine decree is close to the source of things, while divine measure unfolds events over time without end. The divine realm can hold a complete understanding of an endless series without being limited by it, for God is all-encompassing and all-knowing.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00179

Whatever exists through time and change completes its existence in stages here, but exists as a whole in the timeless order. Its existence there is complete, not spread across time. In that order, its amount must be limited, whether its existence unfolds in what we call the past or the future. Material things, considered in divine decree—that is, as they exist in the timeless order—do not come after their matter. The body and its matter exist at the same level there. So if you hear us say that material things are material only in the realm of measure and time, not in the timeless realm of divine decree and God’s direct knowledge, understand what we mean: matter does not come earlier there. We do not mean that matter is absent or that a material thing becomes immaterial in another respect.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00180

The best name for things that unfold in time, when considered as they exist in the timeless order, is “real Forms” or “Forms of divine decree.” These are their complete realities in the timeless order. When considered as things that come into being and unfold in time, they are “created things.” This is a secret that the wise have hinted at. I cannot believe Plato meant anything else. But Aristotle’s followers misjudged him, trusted the stories their own imaginations told them, failed to investigate carefully, and repeated their attacks on the Platonic Forms. The result was that wisdom’s light went out and darkness spread. That is the end of our teacher’s words.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00181

The point is this: all material and temporal things, considered in themselves and in relation to one another, depend on places, times, and positions that keep them apart. But in God’s complete, direct knowledge, they are all present at once. None comes before another in that way of seeing and existing. Nothing there is changing, passing away, or beginning to exist in the presence of the First Reality. In this kind of presence, things do not need matter’s readiness or bodily positions. In this respect, they are like things free of place and time. The early philosophers meant only this by separate Forms, so that their view would not face the familiar objections against it.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00182

You might say: Even if we accept that individual things which come into being have material existence, they could still be free of matter in another respect. But these individuals surely have many different existences. Plato’s followers say that each bodily kind has one separate, eternal individual. That would show not only that it exists apart from matter, but that it is one. And being separate itself implies oneness, as has been proved. So it is very far-fetched to explain their view in this way.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00183

Some people place Plato’s Forms in a separate world of images. This is also wrong for the reasons already given. First, the great thinkers who believe in both separate Forms and suspended images believe in both at once. Second, the Forms are great lights, firmly established in the world of intellectual light. Suspended images, by contrast, have bodily positions. Some are dark, and the wicked suffer when they see them: they are ugly, black and blue images that cause pain. Others shine, and the blessed delight in seeing them: they are beautiful, splendid, bright images, white as hidden pearls.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00184

The Illuminationist philosopher who devoted himself to Plato, his teachers, and the Persian sages agreed with them that every simple kind in the heavens or among the elements, and every compound kind of plant or animal, must have one intellect free from matter. It looks after that kind and is its ruler. He offered several arguments for this view.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00185

First argument. In The Discussions, he says that the plant powers of nourishment, growth, and reproduction are dependent features. The earliest philosophers called them dependent features because they exist in something else; later philosophers did so because their bearer can exist without them. The forms of the elements are enough to make matter into real things; otherwise, elements and mixtures of elements could not exist. If those forms are enough, the three plant powers must be dependent features.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00186

What bears these powers must be either the vital spirit or the body’s organs. If it is the vital spirit, then because that spirit is constantly breaking down and changing, the powers within it should change whenever their bearer changes. If it is the organs, heat—whether natural to them or coming from outside—acts on every organ. Plant bodies contain moisture and heat, and the heat continually breaks down the moisture. Their parts are therefore always changing and wearing away.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00187

When a part of the body disappears, the power in it should disappear too. The remaining parts are then replaced by food. So what preserves the body’s balance as it changes, and keeps it going over time? It cannot be the power or the parts that have already vanished, since what no longer exists cannot act. Nor can it be the power and parts that will arise later: they exist because of the body’s balance, so they are results of what they would have to preserve; a result cannot preserve its cause.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00188

The power of growth arises when food enters the body and disrupts its balance. This calls for movement: the food and the body move in different directions; food replaces what has been used up and joins parts that differ in nature and position. These actions, with their complex structure, exact order, and beautiful arrangement, cannot come from a blind, unaware power.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00189

Plants and animals remain stable kinds. The idea that a plant has a separate soul that governs it is mistaken; otherwise, that soul would be useless, unable to act or reach its perfection, which is impossible. The power called “formative” is said to be simple. How, then, could it shape organs with so many functions for preserving individuals and kinds, as anatomy books describe? Anyone who reflects on this, and on the wonders of living things, will see that these remarkable actions cannot come from a power with no understanding or control. They must come from a power free of matter, aware of itself and of other things. This power that governs plant bodies is called an intellect. It belongs to the level of separate intellects whose members govern natural kinds, sometimes described as the lords of images and talismans.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00190

“If you say: Could the power that acts on and governs our bodies be our rational souls? We answer: We know plainly that we are unaware of these remarkable processes. We do not know when food is distributed among our different organs. Even when our minds are fully developed, we do not sense when it is divided among the body’s fluids, carried to different organs and positions, and shaped into varied forms and intricate patterns. We are even less aware of these processes at the beginning of our lives, when we are ignorant and undeveloped. So our souls are not what carry out these actions. Nor are they made of separate parts, one part to act and another to perceive.”
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00191

Second argument. When you examine the kinds found in our world, you see that they do not arise by sheer chance. If they did, their kinds would not remain stable. A human being might come from something other than a human, a horse from something other than a horse, a date palm from something other than a date palm, or wheat from something other than wheat. But that is not what happens. These kinds continue in the same pattern, without change. What remains stable in this way cannot be based on sheer chance.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00192

The many remarkable colors in a peacock’s feathers do not come, as Aristotle’s followers say, from the different mixtures within each feather. They have no proof of this, and cannot identify what causes each color. How, then, can they make such varied claims without following a clear rule for that kind of thing?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00193

The right view is what the ancients said: every bodily kind must have a light that exists on its own, apart from matter, and that governs, cares for, and preserves the kind. They call this light the universal of that kind. By “universal,” they do not mean a concept that can be shared by many individuals. How could they mean that when they say this light exists on its own, understands itself and other things, and has its own distinct nature, shared by no other?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00194

They also do not believe that the ruler of the human kind, the horse kind, or any other kind exists for the sake of the lower kind beneath it, as though that lower kind were a mold or model for the separate Intellect. They insist that what is higher does not exist for the sake of what is lower. If that were their view, every model would need another model, and so on without end. That is impossible. Rather, because the ruler of a kind is free of matter, it relates equally to every individual of that kind. It cares for them and continually gives them life. In truth, it is the whole and the original; the individuals are its branches.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00195

Third argument. They also argue from the principle that a nobler possibility must exist before a lower one: if a possible being of lower rank exists, then a possible being of higher rank must already have existed. The proof is given in his books.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00196

The world of bodies contains marvelous arrangements and subtle relationships—in the spheres, stars, elements, and things made from them. The world of souls also contains spiritual wonders and bodily marvels in the powers of souls and the way they are joined to bodies. The arrangements, relationships, and order in the luminous world of intellect must be nobler and better than those in these lower worlds. How could it be otherwise? The marvels of order in the bodily world are only shadows and traces of what is in the intellectual world. Those higher forms are the realities and originals; bodily kinds are their branches, derived from them.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00197

Those who believe in Platonic Forms do not say that animal life has one Form, being two-legged another, and having wings a third. Nor do they say that the scent of musk has one Form and musk itself another, or that the sweetness of sugar has one Form and sugar another. Rather, every distinct bodily kind has something that corresponds to it in the sacred world. Each separate light among the rulers of images in the world of pure light has luminous forms from the rays of intellect, along with forms of pleasure, love, honor, humility, power, and other qualities. When its shadow appears in the bodily world, its image is musk with its sweet scent, sugar with its sweet taste, or a human or horse form, with its own pattern of organs and features. These bodily forms reflect the order found in the separate lights.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00198

These are the views of this divine philosopher. They are very fine and subtle, but they do not settle some questions. Do these intellectual lights have the same nature as their sensory images, so that one individual of each bodily kind is immaterial while the others are material? Or is each separate light a Form of a whole bodily kind, rather than a model for its individual members? Accounts of Plato’s views, and the criticisms made by Aristotle’s followers, clearly support the first reading: these intellectual rulers belong to the same kind as their bodily images.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00199

The Persian sages’ practice of naming the ruler of each kind after that kind supports this too. They revered a plant called haoma as the sacred haoma spirit, Haoma Yazad. They did the same with other kinds: the ruler of water was called Khordad, the ruler of trees Amordad, and the ruler of fire Ardibehesht. Suhrawardi, the Illuminationist master, understood the earlier philosophers’ names for these rulers as showing resemblance and causation, not identity of kind. As he says in The Paths, when you hear Empedocles, Agathodaemon, and others speak of the rulers of kinds, understand what they mean. Do not imagine that they thought such a ruler was a body, or had a body, a head, and two legs.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00200

And when you read Hermes saying that a spiritual being taught him, and that when he asked who it was, it answered, “I am your complete nature,” do not take him to mean that it was a model exactly like us.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00201

Another problem is this: if legs, wings, and other organs are parts of an animal’s essence, how can a simple, luminous essence serve as its model, whether we consider those organs alone or together with their luminous forms? A model and what it represents need not match in every way, but what is essential in one must correspond to what is essential in the other, and what is incidental to what is incidental.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00202

A further problem is that these rulers are said to be pure light, while their images are either bodies or dark forms. What do pure lights and their luminous qualities have in common with bodies and dark forms? All lights—intellectual, spiritual, planetary, and elemental—are said to be one simple reality. They differ only in strength and weakness, or through features that come from outside them. Yet these lesser intellectual lights, the rulers of images, have effects with different natures. That follows from Suhrawardi’s view that a maker produces an essence, not existence, which he treats as a concept formed by the mind.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00203

Different effects must result either from differences in what receives them or from differences in their causes. If an effect has no receiver, the difference must come from its cause. But the effects of the Intellects differ, and this cannot be explained only by differences in their receivers: the receivers and their capacities are themselves among the different effects, and they have no receiver of their own. Nor can the difference come from differences among the active lights since they differ only in greater or lesser completeness. Their effects must therefore differ in the same way. This further supports the view that the effects of the Intellects and higher principles—which are themselves luminous realities—must be natures that actually exist, not merely general ideas about them. The different natures we draw from them arise from different levels of existence: stronger or weaker, earlier or later, more complex or more simple. Different levels and relations bring different properties and effects, much as different numbers have different properties even though they are made from units and share the number one. Those who study numbers and the stars know the remarkable effects that come from such levels and relations.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00204
A note
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00205

It is best to understand the early philosophers as saying that each bodily kind has one complete, perfect individual in the creative world. This is its original and source; the other individuals of that kind are its branches, effects, and products. Because it is complete, it does not need matter or anything else to support it. The bodily individuals here are different: because they are weak and incomplete, they depend on matter either for what they are or for what they do.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00206

As you have learned, individuals of the same kind can differ in completeness. Some people argue that if one and the same reality exists on its own in some cases and in something else in others, then if one case needs no underlying subject, none of them should. This is not always true. It applies only when things exist in exactly the same sense. Some forms of existence do not need an underlying subject because they are more complete, substantial, and strong. The most deficient form is an attribute: it is weak and depends on something else. So the fact that one thing exists in a subject does not mean that everything sharing some common reality with it must also exist in a subject, when they differ in completeness and strength.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00207

You also know that the kind of a bodily thing is made real and defined by its specific form alone, united with the final feature that distinguishes it. Matter itself is indefinite; it exists only as the potential for something else. The general kind taken from matter is an incomplete nature, joined to that final distinguishing feature. In a compound thing, the remaining forms, qualities, and beginnings of its distinguishing features are like conditions, tools, and branches of one underlying reality.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00208

That reality is itself an image of the ruler of its kind, just as the other individuals of the kind are images of their rulers. Their relation to it is like the relation of branches to one source. The patterns, proportions, and shapes in bodily things are likewise shadows of the intellectual forms and meaningful relations in their luminous rulers. The ruler of the human kind, called the Holy Spirit—the Intellect that pours knowledge into human beings—stands in relation to the rulers of other animal and plant kinds as images stand in relation to images.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00209

These material forms—human, horse, bull, and other kinds—need sensory matter in our world. But in the higher world they do not need to exist in matter. There they are free of matter, exist on their own, and do not depend on something they are in. Think of mental images: they come from things outside the mind, but exist in the mind as dependent features, not on their own. They can come from substances that do exist on their own. The bodily forms that exist in matter are likewise images of the separate Platonic Forms in the intellectual world.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00210

The separate intellectual Forms are complete in themselves and in their natures, so they do not need an underlying subject. Their bodily images are incomplete and need one, because they complete something else. A mental image taken from a material thing is similar: it is free of matter while in the mind, but not free of matter outside it. In the same way, the intellectual Forms that rule over bodily kinds are free of matter in the world of intellect, while their bodily images—the specific forms of things—depend on matter.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00211

Do not conclude from the word “Forms” that these great philosophers thought the rulers of kinds were created by the First Creator as models or molds for the lower things. A model must be higher than what it models, since it is the goal. But these philosophers insist even more strongly than Aristotle’s followers that what is higher does not exist for the sake of what is lower. They see bodily kinds as images and shadows of higher, luminous rulers, though the two differ greatly in honor and completeness. Besides, why would God need models to tell Him how to make things? And if He needed a model to make the first models, that would lead to models without end.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00212

You might object: Are you not going against Aristotle, the First Teacher, who rejected this view? I answer: truth deserves to be followed. Besides, Aristotle may have been rejecting what ordinary people take Plato and the early philosophers to mean. They often spoke in symbols and figures of speech, especially about this subject, which can leave even eloquent speakers at a loss and exhaust the mind. Or perhaps Aristotle’s wish to lead and rule was shaped by his dealings with people and his time among kings and rulers.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00213

In any case, the book known as The Theology of Aristotle shows that Aristotle’s view agreed with his teacher’s on the existence of intellectual Forms for kinds: separate, luminous forms that exist on their own in the creative world. In its fourth treatise, he says:
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00214

“Beyond this world there are a heaven, an earth, a sea, animals, plants, and heavenly people. Everything in this world has a heavenly counterpart; nothing there is earthly. He also says that the human being we sense is only an image of the intellectual human being. The intellectual human being is spiritual, and all its organs are spiritual. The eye and the hand are not in separate places; all the organs are distinct, yet they are in one place.”
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00215

“In the eighth treatise, he says that what makes the fire here what it is is a fiery life—the true fire. The fire above it, in the higher world, is more truly fire. If it is true fire, it must be alive, and its life must be higher and nobler than the life of this fire, which is only an image of it. So the fire in the higher world is alive, and its life gives life to this fire. The same is true of water and air there: they are more alive than water and air here, because the life above gives life to them.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00216

“He also says that this whole sensory world is an image of that world. If this world is alive, then the first world must be even more alive. If this world is complete, the first world must be more complete, since it gives this world life, power, completeness, and lasting existence. If the higher world is complete in every way, it must contain all the things found here, but in a higher and nobler form, as we have said many times.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00217

“There is a living heaven there, with stars like the ones in our sky, but brighter and more complete. They are not separate from one another as they appear here, because they are not physical. There is also land without salt marshes, all of it fertile. It contains every kind of animal and the earthly nature found here, and plants rooted in life. It has seas and rivers that flow like living things, and all kinds of water animals. Its air also contains living creatures like those found in the air here. Everything there is alive.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00218

“How could these things not be alive, when they are in a world of pure life, untouched by death? The kinds of animals there are like those here, but higher and nobler: their nature is intellectual, not animal. If someone denies this and asks how there could be animals, a heaven, and the other things we have mentioned in the higher world, we say: the higher world is a complete living being, containing all things. It was created by the First Creator, who is complete, so it contains every soul and every Intellect. Nothing there is poor or in need. Everything there is full of abundance and life, as though life were boiling and overflowing.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00219

“The life of all things there flows from one source. It is not just a single quality, like heat or wind, but one quality that contains every kind of quality. It contains every taste: sweetness, wine, and all other flavors; every pleasant smell; every color seen by the eye; everything felt by touch; and everything heard, including all melodies and rhythms. It contains all that can be sensed. These are all present within one single, expansive quality, as we have described. This quality is living and intellectual, and it contains every other quality without mixing them together or spoiling them. Each is preserved in it as its own distinct thing.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00220

“In the tenth treatise, he says that every natural form in this world exists in that world in a better and higher way. Here it depends on matter; there it exists without matter. Every natural form here is an image of its counterpart there. So there are a heaven, an earth, animals, air, water, and fire there. If these forms exist there, then plants must exist there too.”
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00221
The passage continues:
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00222

“If someone asks: If there are plants in the higher world, what are they like there? And if there are fire and earth, what are they like? They must be either alive or dead. If they are dead, as they are here, why would they be needed there? If they are alive, how can they be alive there?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00223

“We can say that plants there are alive too. A plant contains an active principle that carries life. If the principle in an earthly plant is alive, it must also be a soul. All the more, then, the principle in the plant of the higher world—the first plant—must be alive, in a higher and nobler way. The principle in this plant comes from that one. The higher principle is one and universal; the plant principles here are many and particular. Every plant in this world is particular and comes from that universal plant. Whatever someone seeks in the plant world, they find in that universal plant.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00224

“If this is so, then if this plant is alive, the higher plant must be even more alive, because it is the first and true plant. This plant is second or third in the order of plants: it is an image of that first plant. It lives through the life that the first plant gives it.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00225

“As for the earth there, whether it is alive or dead, we will know once we know what this earth is, since it is an image of that one. We say that this earth has a kind of life and an active principle. If the earth we know through our senses, which is only an image, is alive, then the earth in the world of intellect must be alive all the more. It is the first earth; this one is a second earth, like it.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00226

“Everything in the higher world is light, because it is in the highest light. Each thing there sees everything in the being of the others. So everything is in everything, and the whole is in each one. Each one is the whole. The light that shines on them has no end. That is why each one of them is vast.”
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00227
That is the end of these luminous words and noble statements, transmitted by ʿAbd al-Masīḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ḥimṣī and edited by Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00228

These passages clearly affirm Platonic Forms. They say that created things have luminous intellectual forms in the world of intellect, and that a person receives these forms when understanding general ideas. But because we are tied to the body and its obscuring effects, our understanding of them is incomplete, like seeing something far away through dusty, cloudy air.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00229

For this reason, we take realities that are pure existence and light—each distinct and clear in itself—for vague general ideas that might apply to many things. It is like seeing a shape in the distance and wondering whether it is a person, a horse, or a tree. Here, its location makes the shape a particular object, so we know it is one thing among several kinds, though we do not know which one. In the intellectual world there is no location, so what we understand may seem to apply to many individuals.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00230

In short, something seems general when its existence appears weak or faint. That may be because it is weak in itself or because the person perceiving it cannot grasp it clearly. This is what happens with realities that are not material objects we know through the senses. Our power of understanding is too weak to grasp luminous realities and clear intellectual forms directly. Because we are tied to the world of matter and darkness, we see them through a veil or haze.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00231

To sum up: ancient philosophers and their followers said there is a world of intellect or imagination that mirrors the sensory world in its kinds of substances and qualities. Some understood it as a shadowy, spatial world of images. Others said these were forms in God’s knowledge, existing in His own being, as Aristotle’s followers hold. On the ancient view, to say that the Forms exist on their own means that they exist in God, whose existence gives them a firmer basis than they have in themselves. In themselves, they are possible; in relation to the One who sustains them, they must exist.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00232

Some say these words point to the ruler of each kind, the spirit that governs it. Each bodily kind has such a ruler: an Intellect that gives it order and a light that guides it. The rulers are not “universal” because the concept of each one can be said of many individuals; they do not apply to the separate bodies and images as a shared concept would. They are called universal because their care and outpouring of life reach every individual of their kind in the same way. Others say the words refer to bodily forms in this world, considered as they appear before the First Creator. They are fully present to Him and never hidden from His knowledge. In that respect, they are like forms free of matter, time, bodily features, and material veils. God knows them directly, as He knows general ideas and separate realities.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00233

I think the most likely view is that those great philosophers and the greatest saints—who had seen through nature’s veils and reached the goal of human life—taught that forms of things exist on their own, apart from matter. Thinkers and mystics come to know these forms through reason and spiritual insight. These forms must exist. They either exist on their own or depend on someone who knows them. The second option cannot be right, or they would disappear whenever that person stopped attending to them, especially if that person were a soul free of the body. And no one has explained how they could exist inside the knower.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00234

Someone might say that when the soul is not aware of these forms, they still exist in a separate intellect—a storehouse of forms the mind can know. The soul knows them when it connects with this intellect, turns its attention to it, and is ready to receive the forms that flow from it.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00235

We answer: setting aside the problems with saying that true forms are placed in the soul, this view would require a separate intellect to contain many different forms that stand at the same level. That is impossible. Higher realities cannot receive their forms from lower things, since that would mean that what is higher is changed and completed by what is lower. The early philosophers rejected this even more strongly than Aristotle’s followers. So the forms would have to flow from something higher. That leaves two possibilities: either many things flow from the one pure source, or the forms of things exist in God’s own being. Philosophers of the Illuminationist school reject both ideas.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00236

On this view, when the soul knows itself and examines its own nature, it must also know where these forms exist and how they exist there. To know a thing is to have it present to you, not hidden. So the place where these known forms exist cannot itself be hidden. Nor can the way they exist there—the very thing that is supposed to explain their existence.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00237

So there must be general realities that exist on their own rather than as features of something else, and that correspond to material individuals. They can apply to many things because we consider them without deciding whether they are separate from matter or attached to it. When we mentally set aside the matter, individual boundaries, and sensory qualities of material things, we reach a shared nature. Like forms in the intellect, this nature is general. This account avoids the problems already raised. The familiar arguments against a universal existing as universal outside the mind apply just as much to one said to exist within the mind.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00238
A Difficulty and Its Answer
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00239

Avicenna gives this argument in the metaphysics section of The Healing against Forms and mathematical shapes that exist apart from matter. Suppose a mathematical shape exists separately from the shape we sense. Then either there are no mathematical shapes in the world we sense, or there are. If there are none, we could not see squares or circles. But if we had never sensed such shapes, how could we prove that they exist—or even begin to imagine them? We form these images from things we have sensed. If we imagined someone who had never sensed any of them, we would say, as the saying goes, that losing a sense means losing the knowledge it gives: that person could not imagine, or even understand, such things.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00240

But we have shown that many mathematical shapes can be found among things we sense. So the nature of these shapes exists in the things we perceive. Considered in itself, that nature must either match the separate shape in its definition and meaning, or differ from it. If it differs, then the shapes we can understand are not the same as those we imagine or grasp through our senses. We would need a new proof to show that the separate shapes exist, and only after that could we ask whether they exist apart from matter.
